subject: Chemistry
title: Ochre: Humanity's First Paint
description: A quick, practical guide to Ochre: Humanity's First Paint.

hook.text: The oldest known pigment is ochre—iron oxide mixed with clay. Humans painted with it 100,000 years ago.

buildup.text: Red ochre gets its color from hematite (Fe₂O₃). Yellow ochre contains goethite (FeOOH). Both are iron minerals.

discovery.text: Heating yellow ochre drives off water, converting goethite to hematite. Prehistoric artists burned yellow to make red.

twist.text: Ochre was used not just for art but for sunscreen, insect repellent, and hide tanning. It was a survival tool.

climax.text: Cave paintings at Lascaux used ochre 17,000 years ago. The same chemistry colors the Grand Canyon today.

punchline.text: Iron oxide plus clay. The oldest pigment is still in the ground beneath your feet.

quiz.question: What gives red ochre its color?

details.summary: Ochre pigments are iron oxide minerals that provided humans with their earliest paint materials at least 100,000 years ago. Yellow ochre contains goethite, red ochre contains hematite, and heating yellow ochre converts goethite to hematite, giving ancient peoples two colors from one material.
details.whyItMatters: Ochre use represents one of humanity's earliest symbolic and technological behaviors. Processing ochre required planning and chemical knowledge that demonstrates advanced cognitive abilities in early humans.
takeaways: Iron oxide minerals in ochre provided humanity's earliest pigments
Heating yellow goethite converts it to red hematite through dehydration
Ochre use dates back at least 100,000 years in the archaeological record

faq.question: How did early humans discover that heating yellow ochre turns it red?
faq.answer: Early campfires likely caused accidental color changes in nearby ochre deposits. Once observed, the transformation was deliberately replicated. Archaeological evidence from South Africa shows controlled ochre heating in purpose-built hearths at least 100,000 years ago.

faq.question: Besides painting, what other purposes did early humans use ochre for?
faq.answer: Ochre was used as sunscreen due to its UV-blocking iron oxide, as an insect repellent, in hide-tanning to preserve animal skins, as a medicinal antiseptic, and in burial rituals. Its versatility made it one of the most important materials in prehistoric human life.
